newsitem.title: FRANCE: Analysts see Suez, Lyonnaise link-up credible.
newsitem.headline: Analysts see Suez, Lyonnaise link-up credible.

text.p: A link-up between French holding company Cie de Suez and water utility group Lyonnaise des Eaux makes sense and is one of the few options left for Suez to expand, analysts said on Tuesday.
Given Suez' increased emphasis on utilities and infrastructure development, and its limited means, a tie with Lyonnaise would be a good fit, they said.
"The only true future left for Suez is a marriage with Lyonnaise," EIFB analyst Sami Gotrane said.

French daily Le Figaro reported on Tuesday that the two companies were once again considering a link up. The paper said Suez and Lyonnaise have already given bankers a mandate to study the conditions of a deal.
"The objective would be to reach an agreement before the shareholders meetings of June 1997," Le Figaro said.
Suez Chairman Gerard Mestrallet would head the management board of the new company while Lyonnaise Chairman Jerome Monod would head the supervisory board.
Suez and Lyonnaise both refused to comment on the report.

Mestrallet, given the top job at Suez after shareholders staged a vicious and public boardroom fight in 1995, has been selling assets in an effort to return the company to profit and rationalise its wide-ranging and unrelated holdings.

In 1996 alone, Mestrallet was behind the shedding of about 20 billion francs ($3.6 billion) in assets including the 11.9 billion-franc sale of investment banking arm Banque Indosuez, which many believed was the crown jewel in Suez's portfolio.
The effort has paid off and Mestrallet predicted on Monday that Suez would post an 800 million franc group profit in 1996 after huge losses in the previous two years.
Mestrallet said on Monday he intended to focus Suez on utilities and infrastructure development, and retail financial services.
"We began 1996 as a predominantly banking group and have ended it as an industrial group," he said.
The focus on utilities was emphasised late last year when Suez, through its Societe Generale de Belgique unit, took control of Belgian utility Tractebel.
"On paper a Lyonnaise-Tractebel is a good idea," said Jerome Labin, analyst with Pinatton. "Suez must find a financial backbone."
Investors cheered the idea, sending Suez shares 4.7 percent higher to 242.80 francs and boosting Lyonnaise shares 4.67 percent to 560 francs.
Labin added that Suez, in its shrunken state, does not have the means to expand into new businesses.

"A marriage with Lyonnaise is probably not the only choice but it would be logical since Suez is obviously continuing to sweep away the signs of the old conglomerate it used to be," said another analyst in France. ($ = 5.574 French Francs)
